question: Which statement best describes Reconciliation?
options: A unit of work is a single fiber node React processes at a time — roughly one component instance or DOM element. Breaking rendering into small units is what lets React process a little, check whether it should yield, and either continue or hand the main thread back to the browser. This granularity is the core mechanism behind time-slicing: a long render becomes many small steps instead of one blocking task.

The work loop is the cooperative loop that pulls one unit of work, processes it, and then checks whether it has time remaining before processing the next. If time runs low (or a higher-priority update arrives), the loop yields to the browser so it can paint and handle input, then resumes later. This cooperative scheduling — rather than a blocking recursive call stack — is what keeps the UI responsive during large updates.

Reconciliation is the process of determining what changed between the previous and next UI so React can update the DOM minimally. Fiber is the reimplementation of this process: where the old 'stack' reconciler recursed synchronously and couldn't be paused, Fiber represents the same diffing work as discrete, schedulable nodes. The diffing heuristics (type-based teardown, same-type update, key-based list matching) are unchanged — Fiber changed how that work is executed, not the rules.

Interruptible rendering means the render phase can be paused, resumed, restarted, or abandoned entirely before anything reaches the screen. It exists so urgent updates (like typing) can preempt expensive background renders (like filtering a huge list). The major consequence for developers: because render may run more than once or never commit, render functions must be pure and side-effect-free, with effects deferred to the commit phase.

question: Which statement best describes Units of work?
options: Double buffering is Fiber keeping two trees — the current tree reflecting what's on screen, and a work-in-progress tree built during render — with each fiber linked to its counterpart via an 'alternate' pointer. React mutates the off-screen work-in-progress tree and only swaps it to become current on commit, so an interrupted or discarded render never shows a half-finished UI. The alternate pointer lets React reuse fiber objects instead of reallocating the whole tree each render.

question: Which statement best describes The work loop?
options: Interruptible rendering means the render phase can be paused, resumed, restarted, or abandoned entirely before anything reaches the screen. It exists so urgent updates (like typing) can preempt expensive background renders (like filtering a huge list). The major consequence for developers: because render may run more than once or never commit, render functions must be pure and side-effect-free, with effects deferred to the commit phase.

Fiber separates an interruptible, side-effect-free render phase (build and diff the work-in-progress tree) from a synchronous, atomic commit phase (apply DOM mutations, attach refs, run effects). This separation is what makes interruptible rendering safe: all the pausable work happens before any visible change, and the actual DOM update is an indivisible step. It also explains effect timing — useLayoutEffect fires during commit before paint, useEffect after paint.

question: Which statement best describes Interruptible rendering?
options: Concurrent rendering is the set of capabilities Fiber's interruptible, prioritized model unlocks: React can prepare multiple versions of the UI at different priorities and interrupt low-priority work for urgent updates. Developers access it through useTransition (mark an update non-urgent), useDeferredValue (let a derived value lag), Suspense (pause a subtree awaiting data), and automatic batching. Importantly, Fiber improves perceived responsiveness, not raw render throughput.
